## Purpose

This SOP describes the use of competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent
assay (ELISA) kits to screen water samples for bisphenol A (BPA),
bisphenol B (BPB), and selected pesticides (atrazine, glyphosate, and
2,4-D). ELISA provides a rapid, cost-effective immunochemical screening
method for detecting trace-level organic contaminants in environmental
water samples without the need for extensive sample preparation or
chromatographic instrumentation [@goda2000; @aga2013;
@voller1978]. Results exceeding the kit detection threshold should be
considered presumptive and confirmed by an instrumental method (e.g.,
LC-MS/MS or GC-MS) when data will be used for regulatory reporting
[@usepa_immunoassay1996].


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Screening of surface water, groundwater, treated
  effluent, and drinking water source water for BPA, BPB, atrazine,
  glyphosate, and 2,4-D using commercially available competitive ELISA
  plate kits (96-well microplate format)
- **Does not apply to:** Confirmatory quantitative analysis by LC-MS/MS
  or GC-MS (see [SOP-L309](SOP-L309-pesticide-analysis-gc.qmd));
  soil or sediment extracts (matrix effects require separate validation);
  clinical or food-safety testing
- **Location:** EA Program laboratory, SGM 133



## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Lab Manager  | Select analytes and approve kit vendors; review QC data |
| Trained Personnel | Run ELISA assays, record results, flag exceedances      |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |

## Definitions

- **Absorbance:** The logarithm of the ratio of incident to transmitted
  light through a colored solution, measured at the wavelength of
  maximum absorption; the raw output of spectrophotometric ELISA
  readers.
- **Bisphenol A (BPA):** An industrial chemical used in polycarbonate
  plastics and epoxy resins; an endocrine-disrupting compound detected
  in environmental water samples.
- **Competitive ELISA:** An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay format in
  which analyte in the sample and a fixed amount of enzyme-labeled
  analyte compete for binding to a limited number of antibody sites;
  signal decreases as analyte concentration increases (inverse
  response).
- **Cross-reactivity:** The degree to which an antibody recognizes
  structurally similar compounds other than the target analyte;
  expressed as a percentage and listed in the kit insert; high
  cross-reactivity with related compounds (e.g., BPB with a BPA kit)
  can produce false positives.
- **ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay):** A plate-based
  immunoassay that uses antibody-antigen binding and an enzyme-substrate
  color reaction to detect and quantify target analytes.
- **Matrix effect:** Interference from sample components (suspended
  solids, humic acids, pH, salinity) that alter antibody-antigen
  binding or enzyme activity; minimized by sample dilution, solid-phase
  extraction, or pH adjustment.
- **Standard curve:** A set of calibration solutions of known analyte
  concentration used to convert absorbance readings to concentrations;
  ELISA curves are typically sigmoidal (4-PL fit).

## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Chemical:** ELISA kits contain dilute acids (stop solution, typically
  1 N HCl or H~2~SO~4~), enzyme conjugates, and substrate solutions
  (typically 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine, TMB). Stop solution is
  corrosive at working concentration. Review the Safety Data Sheet (SDS)
  provided with each kit.
- **Biological:** Environmental water samples may contain pathogens.
  Treat all samples as potentially infectious.
- **Physical:** Microplate wells are fragile. Handle plates carefully to
  avoid cracking wells or cross-contaminating adjacent wells.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses or goggles
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (change between samples to prevent cross-contamination)

### Emergency Procedures

For stop solution (acid) contact with skin or eyes, flush immediately
with copious water for at least 15 minutes. Refer to
[SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling](SOP-L003-hazardous-materials-handling.qmd).

## Procedure

### General Competitive ELISA Workflow

All competitive ELISA kits in this SOP share the same principle: the
analyte in the sample competes with an enzyme-labeled analyte conjugate
for a limited number of antibody binding sites coated on the microplate
well. Higher analyte concentrations in the sample result in less
conjugate binding and therefore lower color development after substrate
addition. The relationship between absorbance and concentration is
inversely proportional [@voller1978; @goda2000].

### Preparation

1. Remove the ELISA kit from the refrigerator and allow all reagents
   to equilibrate to room temperature (20--25 °C) for at least
   30 minutes before opening.
2. Prepare wash buffer by diluting the concentrate per kit instructions
   (typically 1:10 with deionized water). Mix thoroughly.
3. If samples require dilution (e.g., wastewater with expected high
   concentrations), prepare dilutions in deionized water or the
   sample diluent provided with the kit. Record all dilution factors.
4. Label a plate map in the lab notebook showing the position of
   standards, controls, blanks, and samples. Each standard and sample
   should be run in duplicate.

### Assay Procedure

Follow the specific kit insert for exact volumes and incubation times.
The general sequence is:

1. **Add standards and samples.** Pipette the specified volume (typically
   50 $\mu$L) of each calibration standard, positive control, negative
   control (zero standard), and sample into the appropriate wells.
   Change tips between every addition.
2. **Add enzyme conjugate.** Pipette the conjugate solution into each
   well. The conjugate competes with any analyte present in the sample
   for antibody binding sites.
3. **Incubate.** Cover the plate with foil and incubate on the plate
   shaker at the specified temperature and duration (typically
   60 minutes at room temperature for BPA; consult kit insert for
   other analytes).
4. **Wash.** Aspirate or decant the well contents. Wash each well 3--5
   times with wash buffer (approximately 250 $\mu$L per wash). After
   the final wash, invert the plate and tap firmly on absorbent paper
   to remove residual liquid. Incomplete washing is the most common
   source of high background and poor precision.
5. **Add substrate.** Pipette the TMB substrate solution into each well.
   Incubate for the specified time (typically 20--30 minutes at room
   temperature) in the dark. A blue color develops in wells with bound
   conjugate.
6. **Add stop solution.** Pipette the stop solution (acid) into each
   well. The blue color turns yellow. Read the plate within 15 minutes
   of adding stop solution.
7. **Read absorbance.** Measure absorbance at 450 nm using the
   microplate reader.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
Dispense reagents quickly and consistently across the plate. Use a
multichannel pipette when possible to minimize time differences between
the first and last wells. Stagger plates if running more than one
analyte simultaneously.
:::

### Plate Washing Details

Inadequate washing is the most frequent source of assay failure in
ELISA. Follow these guidelines:

1. Aspirate well contents completely (manual flicking or vacuum
   aspiration)
2. Fill each well with approximately 250 $\mu$L wash buffer
3. Allow wash buffer to soak for 5--10 seconds
4. Aspirate again
5. Repeat for the total number of wash cycles specified by the kit
   (typically 3--5)
6. After the final aspirate, invert the plate and tap firmly on a pad
   of clean paper towels 3--4 times to remove residual buffer


## Data Analysis and Calculations

### Standard Curve Construction

1. Calculate the mean absorbance of the duplicate wells for each
   standard concentration.
2. Express each standard as a percentage of the zero standard
   (maximum binding, B~0~):

$$
\%B/B_0 = \frac{\bar{A}_{\text{standard or sample}}}{\bar{A}_{B_0}} \times 100
$$

3. Plot %B/B~0~ (y-axis) against the log of the standard concentration
   (x-axis). Fit a four-parameter logistic (4PL) curve, which is the
   standard model for competitive immunoassay calibration
   [@findlay2000]:

$$
y = D + \frac{A - D}{1 + \left(\frac{x}{C}\right)^B}
$$

where $A$ = maximum asymptote (zero dose), $D$ = minimum asymptote,
$C$ = IC~50~ (inflection point), and $B$ = slope factor.

4. Interpolate sample concentrations from the 4PL curve. Most
   microplate reader software includes 4PL curve fitting.
   Alternatively, use R:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Four-parameter logistic (4PL) curve fitting for ELISA data
library(drc)

# Example data: concentration (ug/L) and %B/B0
standards <- data.frame(
  conc = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 10.0),
  pct_b_b0 = c(92.3, 84.1, 55.7, 38.2, 12.4, 6.8)
)

# Fit 4PL model
model_4pl <- drm(pct_b_b0 ~ conc, data = standards,
                 fct = LL.4(names = c("Slope", "Lower", "Upper", "IC50")))
summary(model_4pl)

# Predict concentration for a sample with %B/B0 = 45.0
sample_pct <- 45.0
pred_conc <- ED(model_4pl, sample_pct, type = "absolute", display = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("Sample concentration: %.3f ug/L\n", pred_conc[1]))
```
:::


### Dilution Correction

If samples were diluted before analysis, multiply the interpolated
concentration by the dilution factor:

$$
C_{\text{original}} = C_{\text{interpolated}} \times DF
$$

### Reporting

Report results as $\mu$g/L (ppb) for water samples. Indicate whether
the result is a screening (ELISA) value and whether it exceeds any
applicable regulatory threshold. Flag any result that falls outside the
linear range of the standard curve (below the lowest standard or above
the highest standard) and re-run with appropriate dilution if above
range.


## Quality Control

###  Within-Assay QC

- Run all standards and samples in duplicate. The coefficient of
  variation (CV) between duplicates should be less than 15%. If a
  duplicate pair exceeds 15% CV, re-run those samples.
- Include the kit-supplied positive control on every plate. The control
  must fall within the range stated on the certificate of analysis.
- Include at least one reagent blank (deionized water) per plate.
- The zero standard (B~0~) absorbance should typically be greater than
  0.8 (consult kit insert for acceptable range). Low B~0~ values
  indicate degraded antibody or conjugate.

### Between-Assay QC

- Run a laboratory-prepared quality control sample (spiked DI water
  at a known concentration within the linear range) with each batch.
  Recovery should be 80--120%.
- Track control chart performance (mean and +/- 2 SD limits) over time.
- Record kit lot numbers and expiration dates. Do not mix reagents
  from different kit lots.

### Method Detection Limits

The method detection limit (MDL) for each analyte is kit-specific and
is defined as the concentration producing a %B/B~0~ response
statistically distinguishable from the zero standard at the 95%
confidence level. MDLs are typically provided in the kit insert.
Report results below the MDL as "less than MDL."

### Cross-Reactivity

Competitive ELISA antibodies may cross-react with structurally related
compounds. For example, BPA antibodies may exhibit partial
cross-reactivity with BPB, BPS, or BPF. Atrazine antibodies may
cross-react with simazine, propazine, or other triazine herbicides.
Consult the cross-reactivity table in the kit insert and report
results accordingly (e.g., "total triazines" rather than "atrazine"
if significant cross-reactivity is known) [@aga2013].


## Troubleshooting

| Problem                              | Possible Cause                        | Corrective Action                     |
|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|
| High background (all wells yellow)   | Incomplete washing; contaminated wash buffer | Increase wash cycles; prepare fresh buffer |
| Poor standard curve ($r^2 < 0.95$)   | Reagent degradation; pipetting error  | Check kit expiration; verify pipette calibration |
| Sample absorbance above B~0~         | Matrix interference; very low analyte | Dilute and re-run; consider sample cleanup |
| Sample absorbance below lowest standard | Concentration exceeds range         | Dilute sample and re-run              |
| High CV between duplicates (> 15%)   | Bubbles in wells; inconsistent pipetting | Tap plate to remove bubbles; use multichannel pipette |
| Positive control out of range        | Kit degradation; incorrect storage    | Check storage conditions; use new kit |
| Edge effects (outer wells differ)    | Temperature gradient across plate     | Use plate shaker; avoid outer wells for critical samples |


## Waste Disposal

| Waste Type                    | Disposal Method                          |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Used microplate and wells     | Standard trash (after stop solution is added) |
| Stop solution waste (acid)    | Neutralize with NaHCO~3~; drain with copious water |
| TMB substrate waste           | Standard liquid waste; drain             |
| Conjugate and antibody waste  | Standard liquid waste; non-hazardous at kit dilutions |
| Sample waste                  | Drain with copious water (non-hazardous surface water) |
| Pipette tips                  | Standard trash                           |

## Training Record

Before performing ELISA analyses independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete [SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd)
   training
3. Review the SDS for the ELISA kit reagents (especially stop solution)
4. Review the kit insert for the specific analyte(s) to be analyzed
5. Observe a trained operator perform a complete assay (plate setup
   through data analysis)
6. Perform the assay under supervision with acceptable QC results
   (duplicate CV less than 15%; positive control within range;
   standard curve $r^2 > 0.98$)
7. Be signed off by the PI or lab manager
